item.title: 76 years on, CPV spirit abides as commemorations unfold
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 00:09:00
A ceremony commemorating the 76th anniversary of the Chinese People's Volunteers' (CPV) entry into the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) to fight in the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea is held in Shenyang, Northeast China's Liaoning Province on October 25, 2026. Photo: Xinhua "One backpack, one pickaxe, 80 rounds of ammunition, a rifle and a field radio. By the time we had shouldered our packs, the bridge over the Yalu River had already been bombed. We built a pontoon bridge and ran across the river," said Zhou Youchun, a veteran of the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea (1950-53), as he recalled the perilous river crossing faced by Chinese soldiers. Their wartime experiences are compiled in a documentary called Remembering 1950 . The clip from the 2021 documentary was shared by the People's Daily across social media platforms on October 25, the 76th anniversary of the Chinese People's Volunteers' (CPV) entry into the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) to fight in the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea, triggering public revisits to this history. Set to the refrain of a well-known Chinese song, "Proudly, fervently, cross the Yalu River," the clip brought the stories of young soldiers to a new generation as commemorative events were held to mark the anniversary. In Shenyang, Northeast China's Liaoning Province, a ceremony was held on Sunday to commemorate the anniversary. Participants observed a moment of silence for the heroes and presented flower baskets at a monument to CPV martyrs, paying tribute to those who laid down their lives for their country and people. On Saturday, China's top political advisor Wang Huning accompanied Kim Jong-un, general secretary of the Workers' Party of Korea and president of the State Affairs of the DPRK, on a visit to Dandong in Northeast China's Liaoning Province, the Xinhua News Agency reported. Wang, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, greeted Kim at the square of the Memorial Hall of the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea and accompanied him to present a flower basket to the memorial tower. Inside the memorial hall, Kim viewed historical artifacts showcasing the bravery of the martyrs and the side-by-side fighting of Chinese and DPRK soldiers, and gifted a historical photo bearing his personal inscription to the hall. During their meeting, Wang said on the occasion of the 76th anniversary of the CPV's entry into the DPRK to fight in the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea, General Secretary Kim Jong-un's special trip to Dandong fully demonstrates how much the party and government of the DPRK value the China-DPRK friendship forged with blood. Ahead of the anniversary, more than 80 representatives from the Chinese Embassy in the DPRK and Chinese communities and organizations in the country took part in commemorative visits to Pyongwon and Sinyang counties in South Pyongan Province in the DPRK on Wednesday and Thursday, paying tribute to CPV martyrs and honoring their sacrifice. On Sunday, the state Korean Central News Agency of the DPRK published an article titled "Heroic Feats Performed by CPV Soldiers in Korean War," describing China-DPRK friendship as "invincible" and united with "comradely friendship and bloody ties in the struggle against foreign aggressors." The report paid tribute to Chinese soldiers who fought in the war, highlighting the heroism of martyrs including Mao Anying, Yang Liandi, Qiu Shaoyun and Sun Zhanyuan. When spirit outmatches material might At the Memorial Hall of the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea in Dandong, figures on display highlight the vast industrial gap between China and the US in 1950. The US produced 87.72 million tons of steel that year, ranking first in the world, while China produced just 606,000 tons. Despite such enormous disparity in resources and the difficult conditions, the CPV fought alongside the army and civilians of the DPRK, launching a series of offensives, thwarting the US-led campaigns, and ultimately securing victory in the war. Gong Shaoshan, deputy director of the memorial hall, told Xinhua that the bravery of CPV soldiers in life-and-death battles embodied the idea that "less steel, greater spirit" could prevail over "more steel, less spirit." More than 300,000 soldiers were recognized as heroes, and over 190,000 Chinese volunteer soldiers gave their lives. "The spirit forged in the war is a lasting legacy," Da Zhigang, a research fellow at the Heilongjiang Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times. "The victory shattered the myth of the invincibility of hegemonic powers, safeguarded the security of the newly founded People's Republic of China and helped secure a peaceful environment for national reconstruction and development. It also laid a spiritual foundation for the Chinese nation to stand on its own feet and pursue self-reliance." Da said that the legacy remains relevant today as China navigates a complex international environment. It encourages the country to face challenges with courage and resolve, reinforces national unity in overcoming difficulties, and strengthens China's determination to safeguard its sovereignty, security and development interests. It also serves as a reminder that peace has been hard-won and that China remains committed to peaceful development. Bridging history and shared future Shared memories of the war remain a foundation of China-DPRK friendship, while practical cooperation, including the new Yalu River Bridge, gives it fresh momentum, Da told the Global Times. He noted that continued exchanges and cooperation could help sustain the two countries' traditional friendship and contribute to peace and stability in Northeast Asia. During his talks with Kim, Wang said that the opening of the new China-DPRK Yalu River Bridge can be taken as an opportunity to expand personnel exchanges and trade cooperation and better benefit the two peoples. He called for strengthening strategic communication and collaboration to foster a peaceful and stable external environment for safeguarding their respective sovereignty, security and development. The new China-DPRK Yalu River Bridge officially opened to traffic on October 15. The cable-stayed bridge over the Yalu River serves as a cross-border transport link between Dandong and the city of Sinuiju in North Pyongan Province of the DPRK, Xinhua reported. "Seventy-six years on, the bridges over the Yalu River will always remember," Xinhua wrote in the headline of a commemorative article on Sunday. Echoing this sentiment, Lü Chao, an expert on East Asian studies at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times that the new China-DPRK Yalu River Bridge links past and present, transforming the wartime lifeline into a corridor for peacetime connectivity and economic cooperation. Lü said that the bridge would improve cross-border logistics, reduce transport and customs clearance costs, and facilitate trade in agricultural products, light industrial goods and machinery. The bridge could also support economic growth in border areas, including Dandong, and create opportunities for cross-border industrial cooperation and tourism. The improved connectivity could further deepen industrial cooperation and diversify bilateral economic ties beyond the trade of goods, the expert noted. Decades on, the bridges across the Yalu River carry echoes of history and hopes for economic growth, more exchanges, and peace. The CPV's battle cry, "Proudly, fervently," still rings out across generations as a call to press ahead with courage and resolve, and to cherish the hard-won momentum for development and peace.

item.title: Washington's 'shutdown' is choking off its own future: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 22:38:00
China US Illustration: Chen Xia/GT As capital from many countries flows into China at an accelerating pace, US investors - constrained by their own country's rules - can only watch as their window of opportunity narrows. Washington should listen carefully to the concerns of US farmers, pharmaceutical companies and investors, and weigh the costs of imposing restrictions. The US Treasury recently released a revised proposed rule on outbound investment restrictions inviting public comments through December 7. In addition to the existing restricted sectors of semiconductor technologies and microelectronics, artificial intelligence systems and quantum information technologies, the proposal seeks to bring supercomputing and hypersonic systems under more detailed controls, while adding biotechnology to the list and designating China and other countries as "countries of concern." On October 24, China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) responded to "a recent US Treasury proposal that would expand and intensify restrictions on outbound investment in China," calling it a discriminatory move and a typical practice of overstretching the concept of national security. The proposed rules "run counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state," the MOFCOM spokesperson said. China will closely follow further developments and reserve the right to retaliate, the spokesperson noted. The steady tightening of US investment controls is an attempt to contain China's emerging industries by stretching the concept of national security beyond its proper bounds. From the 2023 executive order to the expansion of the scope of restrictions through congressional legislation in 2025, and now the addition of biotechnology, the underlying logic remains consistent: to slow China's technological progress by cutting off capital flows. The irony is that biotechnology, the latest sector to be brought under the restrictions, is also one of the most active areas of mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries. One-third of the world's innovative drugs in development come from China. This year, US pharmaceutical companies such as Pfizer and Bristol Myers Squibb have reached licensing agreements worth billions of dollars with their Chinese partners. Meanwhile, the US pharmaceutical industry has spent months lobbying against Washington's proposed stringent investment restrictions. Under the guise of national security, what amounts to protectionism is first and foremost tying the hands of US investors themselves. Data show that Washington's policy direction is running directly counter to the market choices of most US companies. According to MOFCOM, investment from major sources including the US, South Korea, France and Switzerland continued to grow from January to September, with investment from the US increasing by 7.7 percent. Despite the political noise, most US companies are still putting their money where their confidence in the Chinese market lies. On the other hand, the 7.7 percent growth rate was significantly lower than France's 31.8 percent and Switzerland's 26 percent, showing that Washington's restrictive measures are having a negative impact on corporate decision-making. Member Survey 2026 by the US-China Business Council found that 95 percent of respondents considered their China operations to be "somewhat to very important for staying competitive globally." The direction in which the market is voting of its own accord is precisely the opposite of the direction in which policymakers are trying to pull it. Facts confirm that countries shutting their doors often end up sacrificing their own opportunities. According to the US-China Business Council survey, US exports to China fell 26 percent last year, resulting in the loss of approximately 148,000 jobs. Among US companies affected by their own country's export controls, 61 percent have watched their market share shift to competitors. International Data Corporation predicts that Washington's trade restrictions could leave the US' humanoid robotics market nearly 60 percent smaller than it would otherwise be by 2030. "Once markets are lost, they are hard to regain," US business leaders have warned. By contrast, foreign investment in China's high-tech sector increased 33.8 percent year on year from January to September, while reinvestment of profits by foreign-invested enterprises rose 4.7 percent. The magnetic pull of China's vast market remains strong and continues to grow. As capital from many countries around the world flows into China at an accelerating pace, US investors constrained by their own country's rules can only watch as their window of opportunity narrows. China-US economic and trade relationship is built on mutual benefit and win-win outcomes, and it must not be undermined by the countercurrent of politicization and securitization. The strategic guidance provided by the heads of state of China and the US, along with the cooperative ties painstakingly built by businesses on both sides, should not be eroded by a proposed rule. China-US cooperation is vital to the well-being of the peoples of both countries, to the stability of global industrial and supply chains and to the growth of the world economy. Labeling legitimate business activities as "threats" and weaponizing capital flows undermine not only business confidence but also the foundations of the international economic and trade order. The proposed rule is still at the consultation stage, and its final text has yet to be determined. The rational voices of the US business community deserve to be heard. While reserving the right to take countermeasures at any time, China will continue to counter external uncertainties through high-standard opening-up. The proposition that "investing in China means investing in the future" will only become more evident. Washington should listen carefully to the concerns of US farmers, pharmaceutical companies and investors, and weigh the costs of imposing restrictions. The ropes used to trip others up often end up binding one's own hands first. The simple truth that cooperation benefits both sides while confrontation harms both is one Washington would do well to heed.

item.title: GT Voice: Shipbuilding industry is defined by both competition and cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 21:59:00
The world's first 41,800-ton bidirectional sailing self-discharging ship delivers in East China's Jiangsu Province on July 21. Photo: Guo Yuandanz/GT New data from China's shipbuilding industry has drawn widespread media attention. China continues to lead the world in three key indicators, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) reported. In the first nine months of this year, Chinese shipyards completed 58.05 million deadweight tons (DWT) of shipbuilding output, a year on year rise of 50.7 percent. New ship orders hit 175.29 million DWT, surging 163.2 percent year on year. As of the end of September, the order backlog stood at 399.13 million DWT, up 64.8 percent from a year earlier. Notably, China's new ship orders accounted for 81.8 percent of the global market, MIIT statistics showed. These figures amount to more than a demonstration of the country's manufacturing scale. Shipbuilding is a capital-intensive, long-cycle and technology-heavy industry. When ship owners place orders, they are not simply comparing quotations. They are making decisions on fleet capacity, asset values and delivery security. Choosing a shipyard is, in effect, a vote of confidence in an entire industrial system: its suppliers, engineers, project managers, skilled workers and ability to deliver as promised. China's expanding order book reflects not only the available capacity, but also the market's assessment of its supply-chain coordination and execution. What deserves more attention than the sheer volume of orders is their structural composition. New orders are not evenly distributed across all vessel types, but are heavily concentrated in the segments with the strictest green compliance requirements and the highest technological complexity. In the first three quarters, China's global market share in new orders for green-powered ships reached 74.1 percent, 5.7 percentage points higher than in the first half of the year. This clearly signals that China's leading position in shipbuilding is evolving from the traditional strengths of scale and cost-effectiveness to new competitive edges in green technology, sophisticated vessel construction and industrial synergy. As global maritime environmental regulations tighten and alternative fuel technologies advance, fleet owners are increasingly turning to next-generation vessels powered by methanol, liquefied natural gas and ammonia. Chinese shipyards' remarkable share in green ship orders shows that their capabilities in green design, supply chain coordination and high-standard construction have won widespread market recognition. This advantage is set to prove far more sustainable than a simple cost-and-scale edge. Many foreign media outlets tend to frame the rise of China's shipbuilding sector as a zero-sum game between China and South Korea. But this narrow narrative overlooks the profound changes unfolding across the global shipbuilding industrial chain. The expansion of China's shipbuilding ecosystem has opened up new market space for South Korean component and marine equipment companies. South Korean shipbuilders can leverage China's massive delivery volume and huge supporting demand to expand exports of their high-value-added supporting products. Small and medium-sized South Korean marine equipment makers are accelerating their entry into the Chinese market, with major supporting equipment shipped from South Korea to China including hull safety monitoring systems, marine energy-saving devices and marine engine components. This deep integration not only elevates the supporting quality of Chinese-built vessels, but also gives South Korean companies direct access to the world's largest shipbuilding market. This dynamic of "competition in finished vessels, cooperation in supporting sectors" is far closer to the industrial reality than simplistic zero-sum assumptions. The South Korean shipbuilding industry is facing pressure from labor shortages and challenges from investment in US shipbuilding. Against this backdrop, the value of cooperation becomes ever clearer. Shipbuilding is a long-haul race that rewards sustained technological investment, supply chain resilience and reliable deliveries. Global decarbonization in shipping continues to open up fresh demand. China needs to consolidate its early-mover advantage in green vessels, while South Korea needs a stable export market for the components and a reliable industrial partner. The rise of China's shipbuilding industry brings more diverse, greener supply options to back up the global transition of maritime transport. For competitors such as South Korea, the competition creates some pressure on finished vessels, but it also creates opportunities for component exports, production collaboration and strategic repositioning. So, competition and cooperation has once again proved to be the perpetual norm of doing business.

item.title: Far-sea capabilities on display as China's 48th naval escort formation completes record Gulf of Aden mission
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 21:15:00
The type 052DL destroyer Tangshan (Hull 122) returns to a naval port in Qingdao, East China's Shandong Province, on October 23, 2026. Photo: Screenshot from the PLA Navy WeChat account Cheered by crowds of military and civilian well-wishers lining the pier amid music and flowers, the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy's 48th escort taskforce has wrapped up its Gulf of Aden escort mission and returned to Qingdao, East China's Shandong Province. Its 378-day tour at sea stands out as a fresh marker of the service's maturing capacity for sustained far-sea operations, observers and experts say. Made up of the Type 052DL destroyer Tangshan (Hull 122), the Type 054A frigate Daqing (Hull 576), and the Type 903A comprehensive supply ship Taihu (Hull 889), the 48th escort taskforce set sail from Qingdao on October 11, 2025, and returned on Friday morning. The deployment lasted 378 days and covered more than 150,000 nautical miles. The taskforce safely escorted 423 Chinese and foreign vessels, safeguarding international sea lanes and contributing to regional peace and stability. Gulf of Aden escort operations are the PLA Navy's longest-standing and most extensive overseas military practice since its founding, in terms of routine deployment duration, forces employed, and range of activity, safeguarding national strategic interests, said CCTV News. The 48th taskforce's deployment appears to be the longest yet. In recent years, consecutive escort taskforces have each been at sea for about a year, or at least 300 days, longer than earlier rotations, observers noted. Experts said the reliability of Chinese naval equipment and the level of personnel training have reached a high standard, sufficient to sustain long-term, routine far-sea presence. The PLA Navy has also formed a comprehensive support system combining ships' own logistics with overseas support nodes. The Djibouti support base can provide rest and resupply for Gulf of Aden escort formations and is a key element of navy building. Longer deployments, more capability Throughout the mission, the 48th taskforce combined sailing, training, and improvement, using the open ocean as a training ground. It utilized complex maritime environments and organized targeted drills related to escort operations, including armed rescue missions and round-the-clock helicopter flights, enhancing its ability to carry out diversified missions, according to the PLA Navy. Beyond escort duties, the taskforce took part in the "Will for Peace 2026" joint maritime exercise in South Africa and the China-Pakistan "Sea Guardian IV" joint naval exercise in Pakistan. It also took part in a parade marking the 50th anniversary of Seychelles' independence, paid friendly visits to Bangladesh, Myanmar, and Malaysia, and made technical stops in Oman, Kenya, Singapore, and other countries, according to China Military Online. The 378-day voyage is regarded as setting a new record for a single Gulf of Aden escort deployment, said Wang Yunfei, a Chinese military affairs expert. He told the Global Times on Sunday that multiple recent task forces have deployed for noticeably longer than earlier rotations, with three consecutive deployments exceeding 300 days, a clear sign that the PLA Navy's ocean-going adaptability has improved significantly and reached world-class standards. At the foundation is equipment reliability and seaworthiness. Wang said the formation can continue operating without returning to home port for major replenishment, showing that ship maturity and refined logistics have reached a new level. Comprehensive ocean-going replenishment is the core support. Long deployments multiply consumption of fuel, fresh water, food and spare parts. The capability of supply ships, along with choices of replenishment timing and location, directly determines how far and how long a formation can operate. Multiple taskforces sustaining 300-plus days shows coordination between supply ships and combat vessels is highly mature, the expert said. Personnel support is equally critical. A year-long deployment tests the psychology and physiology of officers and sailors. Rotation and rest mechanisms, mental health support and improved living conditions are the soft power that sustains long-term combat capability, Wang said, noting that a taskforce deployment must have all personnel meet the relevant training standards before carrying out missions. Every post must be ready for any task, training, support, navigation, communications, air and missile defense, to sustain long deployments, he noted. Wider support network Beyond the formation itself, the expert said the PLA Navy is gaining more diverse overseas support nodes for far-sea operations. The Djibouti facility plays an irreplaceable role in providing logistics support for Gulf of Aden missions. Separately, the China-Cambodia Joint Support and Training Center at Port Ream represents another regional node within the navy's broader far-sea support architecture. "China's far-sea support combines accompanying logistics with node-based support, enabling sustained operations of nearly a year," Wang said. The Djibouti base is a crucial support facility for the PLA Navy, especially for Gulf of Aden escort taskforces. For escort formations, the base serves as a temporary home and a key support site, allowing for brief shore breaks, ship maintenance and personnel recuperation, Song Zhongping, another Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Sunday. In the future, the PLA may normalize longer periods at sea with occasional shore breaks, which is a humane consideration and an important way to further boost combat power. Port calls for fresh food, routine supplies, fresh water and other daily necessities all help improve combat readiness, Song said. Ships carrying Chinese military personnel departed Zhanjiang in South China's Guangdong Province on July 11, 2017, to set up a support base in Djibouti. The establishment of the PLA Djibouti base was a decision made by the two countries, according to the PLA Navy. The Ream support and training center can also support PLA overseas humanitarian and disaster relief operations and play a positive role in regional security affairs, Song added. The Cambodia-China Joint Support and Training Center at Port Ream started operating in April, 2025, according to the Xinhua News Agency. At the ceremony at the time, the Chinese and Cambodian sides emphasized that the construction and operation of the center were the result of mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Cambodia, which is conducive to further strengthening ties between the two militaries, better fulfilling international obligations and providing international public security products. Ship support alone is point support; adding comprehensive supply ships creates line support; adding training and support bases creates a point-line-plane integrated support system, Song noted. Strengthening this capability will greatly lift the PLA's capacity to undertake international maritime missions and support its blue‑water navy development. According to CCTV, in 2008, severe pirate hijackings occurred in the Gulf of Aden. On December 26, 2008, the PLA Navy's Type 052B destroyer Wuhan (Hull 169), Type 052C destroyer Haikou (Hull 171) and comprehensive supply ship Weishanhu (Hull 887) formed the first escort taskforce and set sail from a naval port in Sanya, South China's Hainan Province, opening China's naval escort operations in the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia. In recent years, pirate attacks in the Gulf of Aden and off Somalia have declined, indicating that the deterrence efforts of the PLA Navy, along with other international forces, and the joint endeavors of escort task forces, have been effective. From counter-piracy information sharing and commanders' exchanges on board ships to joint escorts, joint exercises and the embarkation of exchange officers for observation, the PLA Navy has engaged in cooperation with many countries and international organizations. This demonstrates an open, confident and cooperative posture, reflecting China's sincerity and commitment to contributing to world peace and security.

item.title: Global Governance Forum concludes in Xiong'an New Area; delegates explore how China's tech advances can contribute to global governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 21:12:00
An attendee tests a robot during the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an) in Xiong'an New Area, North China's Hebei Province, on October 23, 2026. Photo: VCG The 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an), held from October 23 to 25, concluded on Sunday in Xiong'an New Area, North China's Hebei Province, with artificial intelligence (AI) emerging as a major topic of discussion among international participants, who explored how China's approach to AI development and governance could offer lessons for the wider world. Under the theme "Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Reforming and Improving Global Governance in a Transforming World," the forum brought together nearly 400 representatives from political, academic, strategic, business and youth sectors from more than 90 countries and international and regional organizations. Wang Yi, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and Chinese Foreign Minister, attended the opening ceremony and delivered a keynote speech. Hosted by the Chinese People's Institute of Foreign Affairs (CPIFA), the forum provided a platform for participants to exchange ideas on reforming and improving global governance, with AI governance attracting particular attention. Among the recurring keywords in the discussions were practical applications, safety, risks and equitable access. The Global Times observed particularly strong attendance and lively exchanges at AI-themed sessions, where participants raised questions ranging from how AI could be applied to public services and traditional industries to how countries could manage emerging security threats and prevent a widening digital divide. Pan Jingyu, director of the China-SCO Countries AI Application Cooperation Center, told the Global Times that global AI governance is entering a critical period for jointly shaping rules, developing standards and building technological capacity. China has reached a leading position in AI development, Pan said, noting that the emergence of highly competitive Chinese AI models has attracted widespread international attention. Their affordability, innovative open-source ecosystems and technological capabilities have challenged the dominance of a handful of global technology giants, offering Global South countries new possibilities for leapfrogging in digital development, Pan said. Andrea Renda, director of research at the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), believes China's approach to AI development could also offer useful lessons for Europe. "China is a pioneer in artificial intelligence," Renda said, pointing to its focus on applying AI in specific industrial settings and public services, with an emphasis on people-centered applications that improve everyday life. He noted that this approach could be particularly relevant to the EU, where high energy costs and established industrial structures make it important to use AI to strengthen existing industries rather than simply replace them. Speaking to the Global Times about his first visit to Xiong'an, Renda said he had studied the city's development model since the project was launched. He suggested that Xiong'an's experience could offer a blueprint for more sustainable global AI governance, with AI treated as a means to improve people's lives rather than an end in itself. However, he stressed that such a model should ensure local control over data and allow communities to benefit from the value created through technological development. Describing Europe as the "old continent," Renda noted that European cities cannot simply be rebuilt from scratch as Xiong'an has been. Nevertheless, he said the new area offers valuable lessons in energy management, AI, data governance, urban green spaces and the government's role in fostering innovation, which could help European cities find new ways to develop. A foreign guest shakes hands with a robot at the Global Governance Forum in Xiong'an New Area, North China's Hebei Province, on October 24, 2026. Photo: Hu Yuwei/Global Times While many participants saw opportunities in AI-driven development, others at the forum warned that unequal access to technology and growing security risks could undermine its benefits. Lyu Deqiang, president of the Singapore chapter of the Global Responsible AI Council, said the widening AI divide between countries makes fairness in global governance an increasingly urgent issue. He told the media that global AI governance is currently shaped largely by major powers and economies, including China, the US and the EU. Dialogues such as the forum were particularly meaningful because they gave smaller and medium-sized countries, along with other stakeholders, opportunities to voice their concerns and share perspectives. Pan also warned that AI security threats are evolving in two directions as the technology advances rapidly. On one hand, the weaponization of large language models and the use of AI in cyberattacks and defense are lowering the barriers to launching attacks. On the other, AI-specific threats, including prompt injection, model poisoning and unauthorized actions by AI agents, are becoming increasingly prominent. These challenges, he said, highlight the need for stronger international coordination on AI governance. Beyond discussions at the forum, Xiong'an itself offered international participants a firsthand look at how digital technologies can be integrated into urban governance. Some foreign guests visited Xiong'an's digital infrastructure facilities, learning about the city's cloud computing infrastructure and its concept of "three cities in one" — above ground, underground and in the cloud. The city's use of cloud-based data systems in public services also drew interest. During the forum, participants discussed how community-level data could help improve neighborhood management and provide more targeted services for elderly residents and people with disabilities. Some foreign visitors told the Global Times that it was their first time encountering the concept of three interconnected cities, describing it as a striking example of how innovative urban planning and digital infrastructure could be integrated into a city established only nine years ago. Jorge Agudero, a writer and scholar from Spain, told the Global Times that China's achievement in building Xiong'an into a technologically advanced, green and innovative "city of the future" in just over nine years was difficult for many foreigners to imagine.

item.title: Jetta's 'comeback' in China proves the move was right
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 20:04:00
Screenshot of the Jetta M6 Photo: Jetta official website Once synonymous with rugged reliability and the brand that gave millions of Chinese families their "first car," Jetta has recently returned to the spotlight. On October 22, FAW-Volkswagen's Jetta brand unveiled its battery electric vehicle, the M6, in China. Priced at under 100,000 yuan (about $15,000) even in its top trim, the model comes equipped with advanced urban navigation on autopilot driver-assistance features. It surpassed 10,000 locked orders within just 19 hours of launch. This figure may not be staggering in China's fiercely competitive new-energy vehicle sector, yet the market response merits close attention - especially for a legacy automaker racing to embrace electrification. More than just sales performance for a single new model, it points to broader potential for China-Germany automotive industrial cooperation. Earlier, FAW and the Volkswagen Group signed a strategic cooperation agreement in Wolfsburg, Germany. Under the deal, the two sides will jointly roll out 11 China-customized models starting in 2026, spanning battery electric, plug-in hybrid and range-extender electric powertrains. Jetta's electric transformation forms an integral part of this roadmap. More than 30 years ago, the Jetta served as a bridge between German engineering quality and China's mass market. Unlike the old "German technology, assembled in China" model, the new agreement elevates the Chinese side beyond manufacturing and market execution to deep involvement in product definition and research and development (R&D), with the Chinese partner taking the lead in selected areas. German manufacturing expertise and engineering standards, paired with China's mature battery, smart-cabin and autonomous-driving solutions as well as local supply chains, create distinctive synergy. This revives the iconic national car with German roots for a new era. The Jetta M6's market reception serves as a real-world test of this collaborative framework. Beneath China-Germany automotive cooperation lies four decades of integration and mutual trust. Since the establishment of SAIC Volkswagen Automotive Co Ltd in the 1980s, which marked the beginning of joint ventures in China's passenger car industry, the partnership has continued to evolve, with successive contract renewals in recent years and increased investment in local R&D. The rationale behind the cooperation has long since moved beyond its original model. Volkswagen has built in Hefei, East China's Anhui Province its first R&D center outside Germany, with the capacity to fully develop and validate products, cutting the overall vehicle development cycle by 30 percent. A growing body of practice shows that aligned technologies, talent pools, supply chains and market demands from both countries can generate a competitive edge greater than the sum of its parts. Against various external speculations, China has demonstrated its commitment to high-standard opening-up through verifiable institutional arrangements. It rejects closed, exclusive blocs. Foreign automakers receive full national treatment on permits, standards and subsidies. Foreign brands account for one-third of sales under China renews auto trade-in subsidy program. China's Ministry of Commerce has held repeated exchanges with the German Association of the Automotive Industry, welcoming and encouraging German enterprises to deepen their footprint in China and expand local R&D and investment. It also advocates managing frictions and differences through dialogue and consultation to keep the global automotive supply chain stable and unimpeded. Jetta's electric "comeback" in China is a tangible industrial manifestation of this openness. "Volkswagen Jetta, a rational choice" remains Jetta's most classic and widely recognized tagline. Today, "Jetta electrifies, born anew" adds a solid footnote to win-win collaboration between Chinese and foreign automakers in the new-energy age. It is, truly, "a rational choice." Jetta's "comeback" in China proves this was the right move.

item.title: 81st anniversary of Taiwan's recovery commemorated; DPP authorities' attempts to promote 'de-Sinicization' doomed to fail: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 19:59:00
Photo: Screenshot from the WeChat account of the PLA Eastern Theater Command As multiple commemorative activities were held Sunday on both sides of the Taiwan Straits to mark the 81st anniversary of China's recovery of Taiwan, the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Eastern Theater Command released its first poster marking Taiwan Recovery Day, sending a clear message that the PLA would not tolerate or show leniency toward any attempts to separate the island of Taiwan from China and would deliver forceful blows against such actions, Chinese experts said. In an article, the PLA Eastern Theater Command recalled that on October 25, 1945, Taiwan returned to the embrace of the motherland. Taiwan's recovery was an important outcome of the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, irrefutable evidence of the Chinese government's resumption of the exercise of sovereignty over Taiwan, and a crucial link in the historical facts and legal chain establishing Taiwan as part of China. The Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council released a video reviewing how Chinese people fought together in a bloody struggle to achieve victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and Taiwan's recovery. The video also showcased the driving force behind advancing the process of national reunification and realizing the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. On the island of Taiwan, commemorative activities were held in various places. A civic group organized a cultural relics exhibition in commemoration in Taipei, aiming to revive public awareness of history, UDN reported. At an event held at Taichung Park in Taichung, organizers displayed historical materials and photographs documenting Taiwan's resistance against Japanese aggression and its recovery and return to China. The event also featured young people from Taiwan reading quotations and articles left by people who resisted Japanese colonial rule during the 50 years from 1895 to 1945. Young participants from Taiwan chanted, "Return us to our motherland and restore the homeland of our ancestors!" The event was solemn and dignified, China Review News Agency reported. Zheng Jian, a professor at the Taiwan Research Institute of Xiamen University, told the Global Times that the solemn national commemorations and grassroots commemorative events on the island stand in stark contrast to the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities' longstanding efforts to downplay, dilute and distort the history of Taiwan's recovery. In education and public discourse on the island, the DPP authorities have avoided or removed historical facts related to Taiwan's recovery, favored ambiguous wording such as "the end of the war," and deliberately avoided acknowledging the core conclusions of victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and Taiwan's return to the motherland. Through curriculum changes and public opinion guidance, they have promoted "de-Sinicization," whitewashed Japanese colonial rule and fabricated a "Taiwan independence" version of history, deliberately severing the historical ties between Taiwan and the Chinese mainland and instilling a false understanding of history in younger generations, Zheng said. Such historical nihilism is essentially an attempt to undermine the one-China fact from historical and legal perspectives, he said. At a symposium marking the 81st anniversary of Taiwan's recovery held in Fuzhou, East China's Fujian Province, former Kuomintang chairperson Hung Hsiu-chu said Taiwan's liberation from Japanese colonial rule was not a gift that fell from the sky, but a restoration of national dignity won through the sacrifice of countless compatriots on both sides of the Taiwan Straits, who laid down their lives in the struggle. If "de-Sinicization" is allowed to continue poisoning the next generation, how can we face the martyrs who gave their lives for the cause? she asked. Meanwhile, Lai Ching-te and the DPP authorities not only distort historical facts by "only using the term 'the end of the war' while refusing to acknowledge Taiwan's recovery," but also collude with external forces to spread the false claim that "Taiwan's status remains undetermined," in an attempt to pursue "Taiwan independence" by relying on external forces and through military means, Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Sunday. In its poster titled "Remember Taiwan's Recovery, Defend National Unity," the PLA Eastern Theater Command used black-and-white documentary photographs to highlight the historical and geographical ties between the Chinese mainland and the island of Taiwan, as well as the shared sense of pride and national memory among people on both sides of the Straits. A map of Taiwan forms the visual centerpiece of the poster, alongside prominent banners bearing phrases such as "Taiwan's Recovery" and "venue of the surrender ceremony of Taiwan Province of the China war theater of the Allied powers." The poster demonstrates not only China's determination to safeguard the historical facts of Taiwan's recovery and the fruits of victory in the war against Japanese aggression achieved by people on both sides of the Taiwan Straits, but also its resolve to uphold the mission of safeguarding national reunification. Any attempts to dilute historical memory and promote "de-Sinicization" are doomed to fail, Zhang said.

item.title: Chinese research team achieves breakthrough in flexible solar devices
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 19:37:00
Photo: Screenshot from Xinhua A Chinese research team has developed a new strategy to overcome a longstanding challenge in flexible perovskite solar cells, enabling the production of large-area, commercial size flexible photovoltaic devices with power conversion efficiencies consistently exceeding 20 percent, the Xinhua News Agency has reported. Conventional solar panels are typically heavy and rigid. Flexible perovskite solar films, a promising focus of next-generation photovoltaic research, are lightweight and can conform to curved surfaces. However, scaling them up has long posed a major challenge, as both their power conversion efficiency and lifespan tend to decline significantly as their size increases, hindering their transition from the laboratory to real-world applications. The research team, which is led by professor Li Yaowen at Soochow University in East China's Jiangsu Province, has developed a novel research and development strategy called "decoupled co-deposition." The new study was published online in the journal Science on Friday. Li said that co-deposition is a crucial step in producing flexible perovskite photovoltaic films. During the process, perovskite crystallizes out of a precursor solution and attaches to a plastic substrate, forming a continuous film. However, as the film's area increases, the interfacial layer between the film and the plastic substrate tends to become uneven in thickness, as per Xinhua. The team investigated how the interfacial layer forms at the molecular level and identified a competitive mechanism, said co-corresponding author of the paper, professor Xu Guiying. When exposed to interfacial molecules and organic solvents in the precursor solution, hydroxyl groups on the plastic substrate face a molecular "either-or" choice. Some bind to the organic solvents, leaving the interfacial molecules unable to anchor themselves to the substrate. To address this problem, the team proposed "decoupled co-deposition," introducing a decoupling agent to break the bonds between the hydroxyl groups and organic solvents, allowing the hydroxyl groups to instead bind with the interfacial molecules. This helps the interfacial layer adhere firmly to the substrate. Over the past year, the team has worked with a company to scale up production beyond small-scale laboratory prototypes, producing a batch of large-area flexible photovoltaic devices with an effective area of 750 square centimeters. Their power conversion efficiency has more than doubled compared with previous levels, consistently exceeding 20 percent, Li said. "We will continue to strengthen the integration of industry, academia and research, using real-world industrial needs to guide our innovation and steadily advance the commercialization of flexible photovoltaics," Li said. China's installed photovoltaic power capacity reached 1.286 billion kilowatts at the end of July and has surpassed coal-fired power capacity for the first time, making PV the country's largest power source by installed capacity, according to the National Energy Administration on September 1. With the world's largest and fastest-growing renewable energy system, China supplies over 80 percent of photovoltaic modules and 70 percent of wind power equipment around the world, assisting the green transition in many countries and regions.

item.title: China launches new internet satellite group
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 17:15:00
A Long March-8A carrier rocket carrying the 28th group of low-orbit internet satellites blasts off from the Hainan commercial spacecraft launch site in south China's Hainan Province, Oct. 25, 2026. The rocket lifted off at 10:03 a.m. (Beijing Time) on Sunday. The payloads entered the designated orbit. (Xinhua/Yang Guanyu) China launched a Long March-8A carrier rocket from the southern island province of Hainan on Sunday, sending a batch of internet satellites into space. The rocket lifted off at 10:03 a.m. (Beijing Time) from the Hainan commercial spacecraft launch site. The payloads, the 28th group of low-orbit internet satellites, entered the designated orbit. The satellites were developed by the China Academy of Space Technology. The Long March-8A rocket is designed to meet the launch requirements of constellation networks in medium and low Earth orbits. The launch marked the 674th flight mission of the Long March carrier rocket series. item.title: China's national civil service exam registration closes, with over 6,000 applicants competing for a single position: media
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 10:07:00
Candidates exit the exam venue after the national civil service examination on November 30, 2025. Photo: CNS Photo Saturday marked the final day to apply for China's 2027 national civil service examination, with competition for the most sought-after positions exceeding 6,000 applicants per post, chinanews.com reported on Sunday. As of 5 pm on Saturday, more than 6,000 applicants had passed the initial review for a first-level police inspector position or below with the Yanbian border management detachment of the Jilin immigration inspection general station. The position had only one vacancy, putting the competition ratio at more than 6,000 to 1, according to the report. Yanbian, located in Northeast China's Jilin Province, is the only autonomous prefecture of China's Korean ethnic group, according to the Xinhua News Agency. In addition, several other positions have attracted thousands of applicants for a single vacancy. For example, a position at the Gongyi survey team under the Henan survey team of the National Bureau of Statistics had 5,534 applicants who passed the review for just one opening, with six applications still pending review. According to thepaper.cn, citing statistics from Huatu Education, as of 4 pm on Saturday, 3.025 million applicants had passed the qualification review, bringing the overall average competition ratio to 85 applicants per position. In addition, 83 positions had received no applications by the time registration closed. These "zero-application" positions are concentrated in several types of government agencies, particularly maritime safety administrations, railway police bureaus, and immigration inspection stations under border management authorities, according to thepaper.cn. Some positions at meteorological bureaus, National Bureau of Statistics survey teams, and customs authorities have also received no applications. Such positions typically have strict professional or academic requirements and involve demanding working conditions, such as working on the water, serving in grassroots roles in remote areas, or working shifts. Positions in remote and less accessible regions may also attract fewer applicants, as the pool of who meet the requirements is relatively small. Global Times
